title: Domain-Specific Architectures
summary: General-purpose CPUs stopped getting faster for free. Learn why chips now specialize — ASICs, FPGAs, DSPs, TPUs — and where hardware is headed.

blocks.markdown:
A **domain-specific architecture (DSA)** is a chip built to do one job — not general computing — extremely well.

- General CPUs improve slowly now; specialized chips fill the gap.
- Trade **flexibility** for **efficiency**: less general, far faster and lower power at that one job.
- Examples you already use: GPUs, phone camera chips, TPUs.
- This closes out the track — see [gpus-accelerators](gpus-accelerators) for the accelerator most apps hit first.

blocks.subTitle: The specialization ladder
blocks.markdown:
Hardware sits on a spectrum from fully general to fully fixed.

| Hardware | Flexibility |
|---|---|
| CPU | Runs anything |
| FPGA | Reconfigurable circuits |
| ASIC | One job only |

Moving right trades generality for raw efficiency at a single task.

blocks.subTitle: Dennard scaling ended
blocks.markdown:
**Dennard scaling** used to say: shrink a transistor, and it gets faster while using less power per transistor. That broke down around 2005 — smaller transistors now leak power, so clock speeds stopped climbing for free.

- Chipmakers added **cores** instead of raw clock speed.
- Even **Moore's Law** (transistor count doubling roughly every two years) has slowed as shrinking gets harder and pricier.

See [power-performance-scaling](power-performance-scaling) for the full story.

blocks.subTitle: The response: build for one job
blocks.markdown:
If general CPUs can't get faster for free, the fix is hardware built around a single **workload** instead of any workload.

- Strip out flexibility the job never needs (branch prediction, general instruction decoding).
- Spend those transistors on the operations the job actually repeats — matrix math, video decode, signal filtering.
- This is why phones, laptops, and datacenters now ship many small specialized chips alongside one CPU.

blocks.subTitle: Flexibility vs efficiency
blocks.markdown:
Every chip picks a point on the same trade-off: how general vs how efficient.

| Chip | Best at |
|---|---|
| CPU | Any task, low latency |
| GPU | Many parallel simple tasks |
| ASIC | One fixed task, top efficiency |

General hardware wastes energy on parts of itself the job doesn't need; specialized hardware has none to waste — but can't pivot to a new job.

An **ASIC** (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) is a chip designed and manufactured for exactly one function — its circuits are fixed at fabrication.

- Most **efficient** option: no wasted transistors, lowest power per operation.
- Most **expensive and inflexible**: a multi-million dollar design costs nothing to fix after it ships wrong, since the logic can't change.
- Used when the workload is huge and stable — Bitcoin mining chips, TPUs (a type of ASIC).

An **FPGA** (Field-Programmable Gate Array) is a chip made of configurable logic blocks you can **rewire after manufacturing** to implement any circuit.

- Sits between CPU and ASIC: much faster than software for the right task, and reprogrammable if requirements change.
- Costs more power and is slower than an ASIC doing the same fixed job.
- Used for prototyping ASIC designs, and in production where the workload still shifts (networking, some ML inference).

A **DSP** (Digital Signal Processor) is a chip tuned for continuous streams of numeric data — audio, radio, sensor signals.

- Built around one repeated operation: **multiply-then-add**, run millions of times per second on a stream of samples.
- Found in phone microphones, hearing aids, modems — anywhere a real-world signal is filtered or compressed in real time.
- Older idea than GPUs/TPUs, but the same specialize-the-datapath logic.

A **TPU** (Tensor Processing Unit, Google) and **NPU** (Neural Processing Unit, common in phone chips) are ASICs built for one thing: the **matrix multiplication** that neural networks run over and over.

- A grid of multiply-add units passes results directly to neighbors, skipping the memory trips a CPU or GPU would need.
- Huge throughput gains for ML training/inference; nearly useless for anything else.
- Why phones now do on-device AI (photo processing, voice) without draining the battery.

**RISC-V** is an open, royalty-free **ISA** (instruction set architecture — the vocabulary of instructions a CPU understands, see [instruction-set-architecture](instruction-set-architecture)).

- Unlike x86 or ARM, anyone can implement it free of licensing fees, and **extend** it with custom instructions.
- That extensibility matters here: a company can bolt a domain-specific instruction onto a plain RISC-V core instead of designing a whole new chip.
- Why it's rising alongside DSAs — it's the cheap, adaptable base they get built on top of.

Chips are moving from one big general die to many small specialized pieces stitched together.

- **Heterogeneous chips** mix different core types (CPU + GPU + NPU) on one package.
- **Chiplets** are small separate dies combined in one package instead of one giant die — cheaper to make, easier to mix specialties.

blocks.subTitle: Accelerators everywhere
blocks.markdown:
The pattern repeats at every scale: one flexible core plus a growing pile of small fixed-function helpers.

- A modern phone chip already bundles a CPU, GPU, NPU, DSP, and an image processor.
- The CPU still exists — for logic, control flow, anything unpredictable — but rarely does the heavy lifting itself anymore.
- Software increasingly means routing each piece of work to the right accelerator, not writing one loop for one processor.

Common mistakes:

- **"Specialized always means faster."** Only for its one workload — an ASIC running the wrong job can lose to a CPU.
- **"FPGAs are just slow ASICs."** They're a different tool: reprogrammable, meant for workloads that still change.
- **"CPUs are becoming obsolete."** No — they stay the flexible control point that decides what work goes where.

blocks.subTitle: Why now
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why are domain-specific architectures rising now, not decades ago?**

Because general CPUs stopped getting faster for free once Dennard scaling ended and Moore's Law slowed. With free speedups gone, the only way left to gain performance and power efficiency is to build hardware around a specific, high-value workload.

blocks.subTitle: ASIC vs FPGA vs GPU
blocks.markdown:
**Q: ASIC vs FPGA vs GPU — how do you choose?**

ASIC when the workload is huge, stable, and justifies a fixed design (highest efficiency, no flexibility). FPGA when the workload may still change or volume is too low for an ASIC (reconfigurable, less efficient). GPU when the work is broadly parallel but varied, like graphics or general ML (flexible, good throughput, less efficient than an ASIC).

blocks.subTitle: What is a TPU
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is a TPU, plainly?**

An ASIC built to do one operation extremely fast: multiplying and adding matrices, the core math behind neural networks. It skips general-purpose overhead a CPU or GPU carries, so it trains and runs ML models with far higher throughput per watt.

blocks.subTitle: Why RISC-V matters
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why does RISC-V matter for domain-specific chips?**

It's a free, open instruction set that anyone can extend. Instead of licensing a closed ISA or designing a chip from scratch, a team can start from a plain RISC-V core and add custom instructions for their domain — cutting the cost of building specialized silicon.

blocks.subTitle: The core trade-off
blocks.markdown:
**Q: State the flexibility vs efficiency trade-off in one line.**

The more a chip can do, the less perfectly it does any one thing; the more a chip is narrowed to one job, the less it can do anything else — every hardware choice sits somewhere on that line.
